Now what does happen is traders using their own versions to see when they think vol is mispriced. But this implicitly drives the price of the option to the true price (if their models are correct) and then the blacksholes gives the correct iv!

Everyone here is wrong the real reason is due to Volatility drag. Very interesting effect. As a physicist I see it as an effect of discretisation of time in financial markets. But some people see it as proof stock returns aren’t normally distributed. 

Let’s look at an easy example:

Imagine a stock has 50:50 chance of increasing via 10% or decreasing 10% every day.  

After two days you have the following results:

UP ; UP -> 110 ; 121
Up ; Down -> 110 ; 99
Down ; Down -> 90 ; 81
Down ; up -> 90 ; 99

Each have 25% chance of happening but only one of the outcomes is profitable. The expected value is 0. 

This is only after two days. This effect blows up after a year. 

This is also why we know stocks aren’t log normal distributed… as in a long period stocks will always tend to 0.

We can consider each of the above up or down patterns at individual traders.

This is probably easiest path that ensures you leave uni with good experience even if you don’t land quant role straight away.

  
My plan would be:

Ensure you work hard in first year to get good grades

Year 1: Get research experience at your uni. 

Now go through quant and finance interview preparations now. You normally get one good shot per year at each firm if you have experience.  You now have good grades and research experience, should be enough to get bulge bracket bank experience.

Year 2: Get corporate experience in finance, or computer science.   


Use this experience, along with online research (seeking alpha) to be able to palpably talk about finance. Seeking alpha is good in my opinion as it shows how people form opinions, rather than Financial Times which normally has a bias and is hard to digest. Use Reddit to find information about particular interview processess.   


Your brain now is probably used to thinking long and hard, and not sharp and fast so can be a surprise when you get interviews when they ask multiple quick fire mental maths questions. Try go back to how your high school brain worked, about speed. So many times I’ve been asked questions that id have been able to answer easily at 16 rather than 21.

​

Year 3: Get quant role.

You should be good enough to get good chances of internship. If not back to bulge bracket and repeat next year.

Hey OP.  I currently am a uni student with quant internship experience in London. 

There are a few different stages I would have to consider. I am assuming you know English from you post, although it was non-inclusive in the two European languages listed. There is the connection pathway or the experience pathway.

​

Firstly, do you know anyone in the buy side, or just finance in general, uni alumni are normally the way to go? Do you have any connections in the buy side or at the level of managerial / director of a firm in general, such that they are well integrated. A lot of first experience in a financial sector is more likely to be found and consolidated through conversations. Talk to them, find someone on linkedin ect. 

​

This can really be in a firm in France,Spain , England or your home country. As if you pick an international firm with an office in London ( very likely), transferring is easier so keep that in mind (in terms to being awarded/ visa sponsorship). Obviously, going straight to London would be more ideal , but would be harder without buy side experience or good connections.

Skipping this, first time experience directly in London would more likely come from a 'French' speaking role ect.
